title: Neanderthal mortuary and symbolic behavior: observation before interpretation
scope_note: This dossier distinguishes excavated material and dating evidence from behavioral interpretation. Intentional deposition, ornament-like objects, pigments or abstract marks do not by themselves identify a theology, organized religion, deity concept or afterlife doctrine.
epistemic_rules: An archaeological object is an observation; its symbolic meaning is an inference.
Intentional burial is not automatically evidence of an afterlife belief.
Mortuary behavior is broader than ritual, and ritual is broader than religion.
Non-utilitarian does not uniquely mean sacred.
Minimum ages, direct dates and contextual dates must remain distinct.
Species attribution must be based on context, direct biological identification or securely bounded chronology, never assumed from age alone.
Absence of preserved symbolic material is not evidence of absence of symbolic cognition.

claims.claim_text: Modern identification of Paleolithic intentional burial depends on theory, taphonomy, archaeological context and improved field methods; Neanderthal mortuary debates are constrained because many arguments revisit old excavations while new in-situ finds are rare.
claims.scope: Methodological synthesis across Paleolithic mortuary research; not a site-specific behavioral or theological claim.

claims.claim_text: Recent Shanidar excavations recovered an articulated adult Neanderthal close to the earlier ‘flower burial’ location; the authors report that stratigraphic evidence suggests intentional burial.
claims.scope: The articulated Shanidar individual and its depositional context; the inference does not establish flower offerings, ritual motive, formal religion or afterlife belief.

claims.claim_text: At La Ferrassie 8, multidisciplinary analysis reports a pit dug into sterile sediment with the corpse of a roughly two-year-old Neanderthal child placed within it; a Neanderthal-associated hominin bone directly dated to 41.7–40.8 ka cal BP (95%).
claims.scope: La Ferrassie 8 and the cited multidisciplinary context; supports purposeful deposition of this child but does not identify a specific cosmology or funerary theology.

claims.claim_text: Cueva de los Aviones yielded ochred and perforated marine shells, red and yellow colorants, and shell containers with pigment-mixture residues in a Neanderthal-associated Middle Paleolithic context; U-series dating of overlying flowstone places the assemblage at least about 115–120 ka old.
claims.scope: The Los Aviones assemblage and its stratigraphic context; the U-series result is a minimum age from overlying flowstone, not a direct date on each object.

claims.claim_text: The authors interpret the Los Aviones assemblage as symbolic material culture and state that it is possible that roots of such behavior extend to the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans more than half a million years ago.
claims.scope: An author extrapolation beyond the directly observed Los Aviones material; retained for hypothesis generation only and not treated as evidence of a >500 ka symbolic tradition.

claims.claim_text: La Roche-Cotard contains spatially structured non-figurative cave-wall marks whose anthropogenic origin was supported by taphonomic, traceological and experimental evidence; cave closure occurred more than 57±3 ka ago, before the regional arrival of Homo sapiens, in a Mousterian context attributed to Neanderthals.
claims.scope: The La Roche-Cotard marks, cave closure chronology and archaeological attribution; supports anthropogenic patterned marks in this context, not a unique ritual or religious interpretation.

claims.claim_text: The authors conclude that the La Roche-Cotard engravings are examples of Neanderthal abstract design.
claims.scope: The authors' interpretation of the La Roche-Cotard marks as abstract design; abstract design does not uniquely imply sacred, ritual or religious meaning.

hypotheses.title: Some Neanderthal groups intentionally buried some dead
hypotheses.statement: Intentional burial occurred in at least some Neanderthal contexts rather than every articulated skeleton being produced by natural processes.
hypotheses.evidence_balance: Modern in-situ and multidisciplinary site evidence supports intentional burial in particular cases. This does not imply uniform Neanderthal mortuary practice or a specific funerary theology.
rivals: Natural deposition in individual disputed cases
Intentional corpse management without ritual meaning
falsification_or_discrimination: Taphonomic evidence incompatible with purposeful deposition at a claimed site
Stratigraphic revision showing the body was not placed in a prepared context
Independent reassessment of excavation records and sediment processes

hypotheses.title: Some Neanderthal populations produced abstract or symbolically used material culture
hypotheses.statement: At least some Neanderthal populations intentionally produced or used material forms whose patterning is consistent with symbolic or abstract behavior.
hypotheses.evidence_balance: The strongest observations establish deliberate material modification, pigment/ornament contexts and non-utilitarian structured marks. ‘Symbolic’ is a higher-level interpretation and must remain distinguishable from the physical observations.
rivals: Aesthetic or social display not requiring sacred meaning
Functional use not yet identified for some objects
Individual/local traditions rather than species-wide cognition
falsification_or_discrimination: Demonstrate utilitarian production pathway for a proposed symbolic object
Redate or reattribute the context to Homo sapiens
Show marks arose through natural or incidental processes

hypotheses.title: Symbolic material culture predates the Neanderthal–Homo sapiens split
hypotheses.statement: The common ancestor of Neanderthals and Homo sapiens already possessed culturally expressed symbolic material behavior.
hypotheses.evidence_balance: Possible under parsimony but not directly demonstrated by the sites in this pack; convergent evolution, repeated innovation and preservation bias remain serious alternatives.
rivals: Older evidence exists but is archaeologically invisible
The symbolic category is too broad for ancestral-state inference
falsification_or_discrimination: Find well-dated pre-split material with a defensible symbolic interpretation
Build trait models that compare ancestral inheritance with convergent innovation
Test sensitivity to preservation and discovery bias

hypotheses.title: Intentional burial proves formal religion or afterlife doctrine
hypotheses.statement: An intentional Neanderthal burial is sufficient evidence for a formal religion or explicit belief in an afterlife.
hypotheses.evidence_balance: The current evidence supports mortuary behavior in specific contexts but underdetermines motive and cosmology. The hypothesis is intentionally retained as a tempting inference that NOEMA must not silently make.
falsification_or_discrimination: Seek repeated structured associations, offerings or spatial conventions that constrain interpretation
Compare mortuary treatment with settlement and non-mortuary depositional patterns
Do not use burial alone as the discriminating observation

synthesis.headline: Neanderthals cross the behavioral threshold before the theological one.
findings: The selected evidence supports intentional burial in particular Neanderthal contexts, but motive remains underdetermined.
The selected evidence also supports deliberate pigments, modified shell assemblages and abstract non-figurative marks in Neanderthal-associated contexts.
These observations weaken older models in which complex symbolic material behavior is exclusive to Homo sapiens.
They do not, however, license NOEMA to label Neanderthal behavior ‘religion’, ‘spirituality’ or ‘afterlife belief’ without additional discriminating evidence.
Deep-time analysis therefore needs two parallel graphs: physical observations and interpretive hypotheses, joined by explicitly reviewable inference edges.
next_tests: Add dating distributions rather than single-point dates for each site and distinguish minimum from direct ages.
Add competing taphonomic interpretations for disputed mortuary sites.
Map repeated object classes such as pigments, perforated shells, raptor talons and engravings without assuming shared meaning.
Test cultural transmission versus recurrent independent invention using chronology, geography and population history.
Create an interpretation ladder from anthropogenic → patterned → non-utilitarian → symbolic → ritual → religious, requiring new evidence at every step.
